summary: Junior Astronaut: Mars Outpost is a browser-based mission trainer where young players command a Mars habitat for 30 sols. Each turn, they balance power, oxygen, shield and food by recycling water, reinforcing the shield or growing crops. Space weather events, like dust storms and solar storms, arrive with a two-sol warning, so players learn to plan ahead instead of just reacting. Educational pop-ups explain real solar storms using NASA DONKI data, and a “What’s real in this game?” section separates fact from simplification. The game is bilingual (English/Spanish). It answers the challenge by turning real space science into an engaging, decision-based experience. It matters because future astronauts and engineers need early practice in resource management, risk planning and space weather awareness, learned through hands-on play.
details:
What does it do or how does it work?

Junior Astronaut: Mars Outpost is a one-screen game that runs in any browser. You have to keep a Mars base alive for 30 sols (Martian days). Four bars show Power, Oxygen, Shield and Food, and if any bar reaches 0 the mission is over. Each sol you choose one action, like recycling water, reinforcing the shield or growing crops. Every action costs power, so there are no free choices. Every 5 sols, space weather hits the base, using real NASA solar flare and storm records. Dust storms also cut your solar power for several sols. Two sols before each event, a warning panel tells you what to prepare.

What benefits does it have?

It is made for kids 7–12, with plain language.

It needs no download, no account and no internet connection.

You can switch between English and Spanish at any time.

Players learn planning, trade-offs and why astronauts need shielding.

A “What’s real?” panel explains which parts come from real science.

What is the intended impact?

We want young learners to enjoy space science and understand that astronauts must plan for real dangers, like radiation and solar storms, on the way to Mars. The game also shows that real NASA data can become something fun to play.

What tools, languages or software did you use?

HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with no build step and no server.

A canvas for the Mars scene and pixel-art SVG sprites.

Node.js to run self-tests that check the game balance.

Browser localStorage to save the language and sound settings.

NASA OSDR RadLab and NASA DONKI for real data.

Sounds from Kenney (CC0) and the music “Vastness” by Andrew Ev (Mixkit license).

How is your project creative?

It turns real NASA records into game events: real flare and storm dates, a real ISS radiation reading, and real Mars dust-storm science. The look is a mission-control console, with a live camera frame, a mission patch and alarms. The crops need three sols to grow, so you have to plan ahead. A warning always comes first, so a loss never feels unfair.

What factors did your team consider?

Kids first: one screen, short text and no accounts.

Fair difficulty: we tuned the balance with automatic tests so careful play usually wins and careless play can fail.

Honesty: the DONKI live service was not reachable while we built the game, so it ships with real archived events and says so. If the live service works, the game uses it automatically.

Accessibility: it works offline and in two languages, and players can turn music and effects on or off separately.

Credits: we list all data and audio sources, and we state that NASA does not endorse the project.
